props.title: Timecode
props.initialSlug: Four stories unfold simultaneously in split-screen LA

sections.content: Mike Figgis's experimental **Timecode** (2000) revolutionized split-screen storytelling by dividing the screen into four continuous 93-minute takes filmed simultaneously in Los Angeles. Shot entirely on digital cameras, this ambitious project predated the digital revolution while tackling Hollywood's entertainment industry politics. The interconnected stories unfold in real-time, demanding viewers actively choose where to focus their attention. This innovative approach influenced later split-screen works like **Phone Booth** (2002) and **11:14** (2003), while its digital pioneering paved the way for films like **Tangerine** (2015) and **Unsane** (2018).

sections.content: The technical achievement of **Timecode** builds on earlier experimental narrative films like **Nashville** (1975) and **Short Cuts** (1993), which weave multiple storylines through a single city. However, Figgis pushes further by forcing simultaneous viewing rather than sequential editing. The film's use of improvisation within a strict technical framework echoes the work of Robert Altman while pointing toward later digital experiments like **Searching** (2018) and **Host** (2020).

While the film's adultery-and-ambition plot might seem conventional, its revolutionary form transforms the viewing experience into something closer to surveillance footage or reality TV. This anticipates our current multi-screen media consumption habits and social media's multiple simultaneous narratives. Similar themes of watching and being watched appear in later films like **Cache** (2005) and **The Truman Show** (1998), but rarely with such formal innovation. SUBHEAD: Digital Cinema Revolution

sections.content: **Timecode**'s early adoption of digital video cameras marked a crucial moment in cinema's transition from film to digital. While **Star Wars Episode II: Attack of the Clones** (2002) would later grab headlines as the first major studio film shot digitally, **Timecode** demonstrated digital's potential for experimental storytelling. This influenced later digital innovators like **Inland Empire** (2006) and **28 Days Later** (2002), which embraced digital's unique qualities rather than trying to replicate film.
